analysis.one_liner: Narrows when big companies count as employers of workers at franchises and contractors, shielding them from wage and labor law liability.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have limited when big companies are legally responsible for wages and working conditions at franchises and contractors, was referred to committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor and wage law, two companies can be treated as 'joint employers' of the same worker — for example, a fast-food chain and the local franchisee that runs its restaurant. That matters because it lets workers and unions hold the big company responsible when the local operator shortchanges them. This bill would narrow that rule so a company counts as an employer only if it directly hires, fires, sets pay, supervises, schedules, and disciplines workers itself. The bill was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee and never advanced any further before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Franchisors (national fast-food and retail brands), staffing agencies, contractors, and investors who rely on franchise and subcontracting structures would gain the most. Under the bill, they could dictate the terms of business — contracts, branding, pricing, staffing expectations — without being legally responsible when workers at those locations are underpaid, misclassified, or denied union rights. Workers at the small operators in between would face a single, often thinly capitalized, employer as the only party they can pursue.

how_it_helps.text: It would shield franchisors, contractors, and staffing networks from being held jointly liable under federal labor and wage law for conditions at businesses they do not 'directly, actually, and immediately' control, reducing their legal exposure.

It would give companies a clear, narrower standard for when they count as an employer, making it easier to structure franchise, subcontracting, and staffing arrangements without sharing responsibility for workers' pay and treatment.

analysis.who_pays: Workers at franchises, staffing agencies, and subcontractors would bear the cost: if the local employer commits wage violations or illegally fires a union supporter, they could no longer hold the big company above it accountable, since the brand's control usually runs through contracts rather than direct day-to-day supervision.

drawbacks.text: Under current law, a company that controls contract terms, staffing, and branding can be held jointly liable when a subcontractor or franchisee cheats workers on wages; the bill would narrow that liability so control exercised through contracts no longer counts, letting large companies benefit from that control without bearing responsibility for it.

The bill would amend both the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act, so workers losing wage claims would also lose union-related protections against the parent company, not just back-pay remedies.

Supporters' good-faith argument: the current broader standard makes franchisors and contractors liable for employment decisions they did not directly make, which they argue raises costs and discourages local franchising.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given franchisors, contractors, and investors clear protection from liability for wages and labor conditions at businesses they control through contracts, cutting their legal costs and compliance exposure. But the cost falls on workers: when a franchisee cannot pay owed wages or unlawfully fires a union supporter, the workers would have no claim against the deep-pocketed company that wrote the operating rules. Since the bill died in committee without action, no one bears these effects; the outcome preserves the status quo in which workers can reach the company above their direct employer.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it sat without a markup or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House introduced the bill on April 25, 2023 and referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce, the only action it ever received.
No committee markup, hearing vote, or floor vote on the bill is recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Franchisors, staffing agencies, and investors who use franchise and contract structures are better off: the broader joint-employer rules they lobbied against remain unsettled but were never locked into statute either, and no new liability limits took effect.

for.name: Rep. James Comer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to narrow joint-employer liability under federal labor and wage law.

for.name: House Education and Workforce Committee leadership
for.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without a markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 92 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, and the bill never advanced past the Republican-run committee.

industries.note: The bill would cut off joint-employer liability, so a brand could dictate operations at franchise locations without being responsible for wage theft or labor violations there. Workers would bear the risk when franchisees cannot pay.
A narrower joint-employer test reduces the chance that client companies share responsibility for temporary and contract workers' pay and conditions, keeping the client insulated from labor claims.
Small franchisees would remain the sole legal employer, avoiding shared liability, though critics note the bill lets the national brand keep control while shouldering none of it.
